group.title: Media and advertising
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: The amount of time given to a subject or ad on TV or radio.
examples: The new party got very little {airtime} during the campaign.
wrong: With so much airtime, the story was never on TV.

words.meaning: How well people know and recognize a company’s name and products.
examples: The ads raised {brand awareness} among young buyers.
wrong: Thanks to its brand awareness, nobody had heard of the company.

words.meaning: A person who decides what goes into a newspaper or magazine and corrects it.
examples: The {editor} cut my article from 900 words to 500.
wrong: The editor never reads anything before it is printed.

words.meaning: An ad written to look like a normal news article.
examples: The health article was really an {advertorial} paid for by the drug company.
wrong: The advertorial was a news report that nobody paid for.

words.meaning: Showing a brand’s goods in a film or show in return for payment.
examples: The hero drinking the same soda in every scene is {product placement}.
wrong: It was product placement because no brand appeared anywhere.

words.meaning: To change a photo so a person looks more perfect than in real life.
examples: The model’s skin was {airbrushed} to remove every line.
wrong: They airbrushed the photo, so it shows every real flaw.

words.meaning: A person who makes videos, posts or other material to share online.
examples: As a {content creator}, she uploads a cooking video every day.
wrong: The content creator has never made or posted anything.

words.meaning: A long TV ad that looks like a show and explains a product.
examples: Late at night, the channel shows a thirty-minute {infomercial} for kitchen knives.
wrong: The infomercial was a ten-second ad with no information at all.

words.meaning: To mention a product or event on air or online to make people buy it.
examples: The singer came on the show to {plug} her new album.
wrong: He plugged his book by never mentioning it once.

words.meaning: A way of life focused on buying more and more things.
examples: Critics say holiday ads feed {consumerism}.
wrong: His consumerism meant he hardly bought anything at all.

words.meaning: To refuse to buy or use something as a protest.
examples: Shoppers {boycotted} the brand after the offensive ad.
wrong: They boycotted the shop by buying everything in it.

words.meaning: To remove parts of something that people in power think are unacceptable.
examples: The government {censored} the film’s violent scenes.
wrong: They censored the book by printing every word of it.

words.meaning: A company or person that pays for ads.
examples: The magazine lost several big {advertisers} after the scandal.
wrong: The advertiser never pays for any ads.

words.meaning: A person with many online followers who can affect what they buy or think.
examples: The {influencer} posted a video about the new trainers.
wrong: The influencer has no followers and nobody listens to her.

words.meaning: To pay for an event or program in return for advertising.
examples: A bank {sponsors} the city marathon.
wrong: The company sponsored the event by refusing to give any money.

words.meaning: Money a company gives to support something in return for advertising.
examples: The team’s shirt {sponsorship} brings in millions.
wrong: With no sponsorship, the company paid for everything.

words.meaning: Public support for a product by a famous person, often for money.
examples: The athlete earns more from {endorsements} than from racing.
wrong: Her endorsement was a public warning not to buy the product.

words.meaning: An advertisement on television or radio.
examples: They show a lot of {commercials} during the big game.
wrong: The commercial was a news report with no products in it.

words.meaning: A short, easy-to-remember phrase used in advertising.
examples: The company’s {slogan} is ’Simply better’.
wrong: Their slogan is a long, forgettable paragraph.

words.meaning: The particular group of people an ad or product is meant for.
examples: Teenagers are the {target audience} for this game.
wrong: The ad ignored its target audience completely and reached it perfectly.

words.meaning: Attention from the media and the public.
examples: The scandal gave the band a lot of {publicity}.
wrong: The famous launch got publicity, so nobody heard about it.

words.meaning: A very large board by a road for advertisements.
examples: A huge {billboard} by the highway shows the new phone.
wrong: The billboard is so small you need glasses to see it.

words.meaning: A small printed paper with an ad, handed out or posted.
examples: They handed out {flyers} for the concert.
wrong: The flyer was a huge sign on top of a skyscraper.

words.meaning: So bright or unusual that people notice it at once.
examples: The poster used {eye-catching} colors to stand out.
wrong: The eye-catching ad was so dull that nobody noticed it.

words.meaning: A short, simple tune used in a radio or TV ad.
examples: Everyone knows the {jingle} from that cereal ad.
wrong: The jingle was a long, silent written report.

words.meaning: A small design that a company uses as its symbol.
examples: The company’s {logo} is a red apple.
wrong: The logo is the price written on the receipt.

words.meaning: A person who pays regularly to get a magazine or service.
examples: The channel now has a million {subscribers}.
wrong: As a subscriber, he never receives the magazine.

words.meaning: A short pause in a TV or radio show when ads are played.
examples: I made tea during the {commercial break}.
wrong: During the commercial break, the show went on with no ads.

words.meaning: Numbers that show how many people watch a TV program.
examples: The show’s {ratings} fell after the second season.
wrong: High ratings meant nobody was watching the show.

words.meaning: The evening hours when most people watch television.
examples: The final is on at {prime time}, so millions will watch.
wrong: Prime time is the early morning hour when nobody watches TV.

words.meaning: Too much excited talk in the media to make something seem important.
examples: After all the {hype}, the film was a disappointment.
wrong: There was a lot of hype, so nobody had heard of the film.

words.meaning: A constantly updated list of posts and stories on an app or website.
examples: I scrolled through my {news feed} on the bus.
wrong: The news feed never changes and shows the same post forever.

words.meaning: An ad that suddenly opens in a new window on a website.
examples: I installed a blocker to stop every {pop-up ad}.
wrong: The pop-up ad stayed hidden and never appeared on screen.

words.meaning: Online content with a shocking title made to get people to click.
examples: ’You won’t believe what happened next’ is classic {clickbait}.
wrong: The clickbait headline was dull and gave the full story.

words.meaning: Very popular online at the moment.
examples: The video is {trending} on social media.
wrong: The hashtag was trending because nobody used it.

words.meaning: To make something widely known to the public.
examples: They used posters to {publicize} the festival.
wrong: She publicized the event by keeping it a secret.

words.meaning: The work of advertising and selling a product.
examples: The film’s {marketing} cost more than the film itself.
wrong: Marketing means hiding a product so nobody buys it.

words.meaning: Giving a wrong idea or impression.
examples: The ad was {misleading} about the price.
wrong: The misleading sign told us exactly the right way.

words.meaning: Written to shock or excite people rather than inform them.
examples: The paper used a {sensational} headline to sell copies.
wrong: The sensational report was calm and carefully balanced.

words.meaning: The first page of a newspaper, with the most important news.
examples: The scandal was on the {front page} of every paper.
wrong: The front page is the last page, at the very back of the paper.
